The early life history of Teredo navalis begins with a trochophore larva measuring approximately 0.005 cm  in length at the moment of hatching from the egg capsule. Gastrulation is completed within one day  at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], at which point the trochophore hatches and becomes free-swimming; this remarkably brief development from fertilisation to eclosion is consistent with the high metabolic rates characteristic of warm-water bivalve larvae. Following hatching, the larva continues to develop and begins to feed exogenously once it transforms into a umboveliger, an event that occurs at a shell length of about 0.012 cm [Lb = about 0.012 cm]. The age at which this feeding-capable umboveliger stage is attained is approximately nine days [ab = approximately nine days] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], marking the trophic switch from reliance on yolk reserves to planktotrophic feeding on phytoplankton. At birth, defined as the moment the larva becomes a feeding umboveliger, the wet weight of an individual is a minuscule 0.00000013 grams [Wwb = 0.00000013 grams], a value derived from the typical dimensions of the larva, which are roughly 75 to 88 micrometers long and 55 to 57 micrometers wide.

After the initial planktotrophic phase, the umboveliger larvae of Teredo navalis undergo a period of pelagic larval dispersal. Observations of released larvae from the gill chamber of brooding females indicate that the veliger stage, including the umboveliger, persists for an average of 21 days before the larva becomes competent to settle. Following this dispersal interval, the larva then requires an average of 17 days to complete larval metamorphosis, a process involving the loss of the velum and the acquisition of rasping ridges on the shell that are essential for boring into wood. The total duration from birth to the end of metamorphosis and settlement is therefore calculated at 51 days , a value measured under field conditions where the mean temperature during this period was 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. At the conclusion of metamorphosis, the body length of the newly settled juvenile is 0.1 cm , marking the transition to a burrowing lifestyle within the wooden substratum. This extended larval period, while energetically costly, allows for wide spatial dispersal and colonization of new habitats.

Following successful settlement and metamorphosis, the young juvenile of Teredo navalis enters a rapid growth phase as it bores into and consumes the surrounding wood. Field observations at Woods Hole indicate that after settlement, the time required for an individual to reach puberty is approximately 8 weeks, or 56 days [tp = 56 days], at a mean water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. At this pubertal stage, the total body length of the individual is 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm], and the corresponding dry weight at puberty is 0.01 grams . This moderately fast maturation, relative to many other marine bivalves, is likely an adaptation to exploit ephemeral wood substrata in the marine environment. The wet weight of an adult individual that has reached its ultimate size can be substantial; computed from a maximum length of 60 cm and a body diameter of roughly 1 cm, the ultimate wet weight is approximately 47 grams [Wwi = approximately 47 grams], representing a dramatic increase of several orders of magnitude from the birth weight.

Reproductive output in Teredo navalis is considerable, reflecting the species' role as an opportunistic colonizer of sunken driftwood and wooden maritime structures. At a water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], a reproductively active female can spawn between three and four times within a single season. During each spawning event, she releases a large number of eggs, typically ranging from 2.5 million to 3.3 million eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.5 million to 3.3 million eggs per clutch]. Given that three to four such spawning events occur per season [F_R_i = three to four such spawning events occur per season], the total seasonal fecundity is exceptionally high, a reproductive strategy common among marine invertebrates that broadcast their gametes into the water column where fertilization success is uncertain. The ultimate total length that an individual can attain is 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], making Teredo navalis one of the largest wood-boring bivalves. This remarkable size, coupled with its high fecundity, explains the significant economic damage this species inflicts on submerged wooden pilings and ships.

Longevity in Teredo navalis is strongly modulated by environmental temperature, a pattern observed across many ectothermic marine organisms. In cooler waters, such as those typical of northern Atlantic habitats with a mean temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years]. In contrast, at a slightly elevated mean temperature of 11.5 °C [T = 11.5 °C], the documented lifespan is reduced to about 730 days [am = about 730 days]. This inverse relationship between temperature and lifespan is a well-known physiological phenomenon linked to accelerated metabolic rates and higher rates of cellular damage accumulation at warmer temperatures. The species itself is a highly specialized wood-boring bivalve belonging to the family Teredinidae, and it is widely distributed across temperate and tropical oceans. Its ability to digest cellulose through symbiotic bacteria housed in its gills allows it to occupy a unique ecological niche, converting woody debris into animal biomass and contributing to nutrient cycling in coastal marine environments. The combination of a long, dispersive larval phase and a high reproductive rate makes Teredo navalis a highly successful invasive species in many parts of the world.
